name: Banjul
subtitle: Banjul, capital of Gambia: its numbers, a short history and places to see beyond the World Heritage list.

keyPoints.text: About 31,054 people live in the Banjul local government area (the island city) (counted 2013).
On 23 April 1816 Captain Alexander Grant made a treaty with the king of Kombo, Tomani Bojang, leasing the island to the British for 103 iron bars a year.
The lease was paid as a yearly sum of 103 iron bars.

parts.text: On 23 April 1816 Captain Alexander Grant made a treaty with the king of Kombo, Tomani Bojang, leasing the island to the British for 103 iron bars a year.
The lease was paid as a yearly sum of 103 iron bars.
The settlement was named Bathurst after the British Colonial Secretary, and the island before 1816 was known to the Portuguese as Banjulo.
In the 1980s, after a period of stagnation, many residents left Banjul for the Kombos, creating the Greater Banjul area.
In the 2013 census Banjul had the smallest share of the national population of any local government area, 1.6 percent.
Banjul had the lowest share of females of any local government area in 2013, at 48.9 percent.
Banjul municipality is the seat of government of The Gambia.
Banjul and Kanifing are entirely urban, with no rural strata, in the 2013 survey design.
Comparing the 2013 and 2024 censuses, Banjul was the only local government area whose population declined (by 15 percent).
The Gambia Ports Authority took over cargo handling in the port of Banjul from 1 January 1973.
The museum's ground floor is dedicated to an exhibition on Banjul's history called 'Banjul, Bathurst, Banjul'.

parts.text: 31,054 in 2013, according to the figures compiled from the national statistics office. Which area is counted matters: Banjul Local Government Area (Banjul City Council), the island city, 2013 census, both sexes.

items.text: Portuguese navigators entered the mouth of the Gambia River in 1455 and were driven off by hostile locals.
Captain Alexander Grant concluded a treaty with Tomani Bojang, king of Kombo, for the island on 23 April 1816.
The name Bathurst symbolised British colonial rule over the island from 1816 to 1965.
The Gambia Ports Authority began operating on 1 July 1972.
The National Museum was created in 1985 by the first ministry of culture.
Arch 22 was built between 1995 and 1996 at a cost of US$1 million.
The 2013 census counted 31,054 people in Banjul.
After the fall of Yahya Jammeh in January 2017 the 'unknown soldier' statue from Arch 22 was removed and later relocated to the National Museum.
